units.text: When several prefix fields are to be output, the order is always file name, line number, and byte offset, regardless of the order in which these options were specified.
units.sourceHTML: When several prefix fields are to be output, the order is always file name, line number, and byte offset, regardless of the order in which these options were specified.

units.text: Print the 0-based byte offset within the input file before each line of output. If ⟦0⟧ (⟦1⟧) is specified, print the offset of the matching part itself.
units.sourceHTML: Print the 0-based byte offset within the input file before each line of output. If -o (--only-matching) is specified, print the offset of the matching part itself.

units.text: Print the file name for each match. This is the default when there is more than one file to search.
units.sourceHTML: Print the file name for each match. This is the default when there is more than one file to search.

units.text: Suppress the prefixing of file names on output. This is the default when there is only one file (or only standard input) to search.
units.sourceHTML: Suppress the prefixing of file names on output. This is the default when there is only one file (or only standard input) to search.

units.text: Prefix each line of output with the 1-based line number within its input file. (⟦0⟧ is specified by POSIX.)
units.sourceHTML: Prefix each line of output with the 1-based line number within its input file. (-n is specified by POSIX.)

units.text: Make sure that the first character of actual line content lies on a tab stop, so that the alignment of tabs looks normal. This is useful with options that prefix their output to the actual content: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and ⟦2⟧. This may also prepend spaces to output line numbers and byte offsets so that lines from a single file all start at the same column.
units.sourceHTML: Make sure that the first character of actual line content lies on a tab stop, so that the alignment of tabs looks normal. This is useful with options that prefix their output to the actual content: -H, -n, and -b. This may also prepend spaces to output line numbers and byte offsets so that lines from a single file all start at the same column.

units.text: Output a zero byte (the ASCII NUL character) instead of the character that normally follows a file name. For example, ‘⟦0⟧’ outputs a zero byte after each file name instead of the usual newline. This option makes the output unambiguous, even in the presence of file names containing unusual characters like newlines. This option can be used with commands like ‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, ‘⟦3⟧’, and ‘⟦4⟧’ to process arbitrary file names, even those that contain newline characters.
units.sourceHTML: Output a zero byte (the ASCII NUL character) instead of the character that normally follows a file name. For example, ‘grep -lZ’ outputs a zero byte after each file name instead of the usual newline. This option makes the output unambiguous, even in the presence of file names containing unusual characters like newlines. This option can be used with commands like ‘find -print0’, ‘perl -0’, ‘sort -z’, and ‘xargs -0’ to process arbitrary file names, even those that contain newline characters.
